title: A Life in Shapes
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Abstraction, design and a life

hero.credit: Hilma af Klint, *The Ten Largest, No. 1, Childhood*, Group IV, 1907. Hilma af Klint Foundation. Public domain

objective: Students look closely at the painting on poster 1, Hilma af Klint’s *The Ten Largest, No. 1, Childhood* (1907), and describe it by its shapes, lines and colors before they learn its title. They learn that af Klint never showed her abstract paintings in an exhibition, and connect that to poster 1’s words about overlooked artists. They then read how poster 2’s designer told Violet Dina Want’s life, and make an abstract work of their own that stands for one part of a life.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Art does not have to show a face to be about a person. Learning to read shapes and colors, and to use them on purpose, gives you a way to say what words and photographs can’t.

materials: The painting and both posters on a screen, or page 3 of this plan
Colored pencils, crayons or paint; paper
questions: Cover the title. What do you think the painting is about? Now read it: *Childhood*. What changes?
Why might a museum put an abstract painting on a poster about women’s history?
Poster 2 shows Violet in photographs. What could an abstract painting of her life show that a photograph can’t?
Which artists, inventors or writers might be overlooked today?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **In the exhibition,** poster 1 carries af Klint’s painting; poster 2 tells Violet’s life. **Online,** the *Violet’s Life* room gives each part of her life a keepsake.

steps.title: Look first
script: Project the painting for a full minute, with no title. Ask: *“What do you see? What could a painting like this be about?”* Take every answer. Then give the title: *The Ten Largest, No. 1, Childhood*. Ask whether it changes what they see. One more fact to hold on to: af Klint painted it in **1907**, the year Violet Dina Want, the woman on poster 2, was born.

screen.alt: A painting by Hilma af Klint: on a deep blue ground, a ring of pale, petal-like flowers with orange and yellow centers and white ovals holding pink rose discs, above looping orange lines like handwriting around a pale violet circle ringed with yellow, and a row of yellow, blue and white circles along the foot

steps.purpose: Look before knowing: let the shapes and colors work before the title does.
students: What do you see? What could a painting like this be about?
Which shape or color do you notice first?

steps.title: Shape, line, color
script: **The elements.** Name what students found: ovals and circles, petal shapes in a ring, curling lines that loop like handwriting, bright colors on a deep blue ground, a row of small circles along the foot. None of it is a picture of a child. Ask how a painting with no child in it can still be called *Childhood*.

cells: Ovals, circles, petal shapes, a ring
What do the lines remind you of?
Bright colors on a deep blue ground
Which color pulls your eye first?
Does the title change what you see?

steps.purpose: Give students the words to describe what they saw.
students: Name one shape, one line and one color, and where each is.

steps.title: Hilma af Klint
script: **The artist.** Read poster 1’s words: *“The painting is by Hilma af Klint, a Swedish artist born in 1862. Between August and December 1907 she painted a series of huge works, made of ovals, circles and curling lines in bright colors. By the time she died in 1944, she had never shown any of her abstract paintings in an exhibition.”* Poster 1 also says women’s lives are understood *“not just through the contributions of overlooked inventors, activists, artists, and writers, but also through the everyday lives of ordinary women.”* The exhibition does not say why she kept her work back; let students ask.

screen.text: The painting is by Hilma af Klint, a Swedish artist born in 1862. Between August and December 1907 she painted a series of huge works, made of ovals, circles and curling lines in bright colors. By the time she died in 1944, she had never shown any of her abstract paintings in an exhibition.

steps.purpose: Meet the artist, and the fact that she never showed this kind of work.
students: Why might an artist not show her work?
What do we lose when an artist is overlooked?

steps.title: A life in a poster
script: **A life in a poster.** Show poster 2. Its designer tells Violet’s life in decorative lettering for her name, her biography in typewriter text, and four family photographs set as strips of film negative. The *Violet’s Life* room goes further: it gives each part of her life a small drawn keepsake, a house, a sewing machine, a coat, a piano, a rose. One woman’s life, told three ways: photographs, words and symbols.

steps.purpose: See how a designer told one woman’s life with lettering, text and photographs.
students: Why set the photographs as strips of film negative?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three look closely at the painting, then make an abstract work for one part of a life.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find shapes, lines and colors in af Klint’s painting with a checklist, then choose three shapes and three colors for their own childhood and make a small abstract work with them.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Describe the painting element by element, compare it with poster 2’s photographs, then choose one of Violet’s keepsakes and make an abstract panel for that part of her life, with an artist’s statement.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Ask how an artist can be overlooked, analyze poster 2’s design choices, then design a poster panel for a woman in their own family or community: an abstract painting, her name in lettering of their own, and three keepsake symbols, with a rationale.

steps.purpose: Look closely, then make an abstract work for a part of a life, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three look closely at af Klint’s painting, then make a work of your own.

steps.title: A gallery with no faces
script: Lay the work out as a gallery. Each student guesses one classmate’s meaning from the shapes and colors alone, then hears it. Close with: *“If one painting had to stand for your childhood, with no faces and no words, what would be in it?”*

screen.question: If one painting had to stand for your childhood, with no faces and no words, what would be in it?

steps.purpose: Read each other’s work by its elements before hearing its meaning.
students: Guess a classmate’s meaning from their shapes and colors.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back: *“Can you now…?”* Thumbs up, sideways or down; ask a Red Level student to answer the last.
